BASC Attention Problems assess tendencies to be easily distracted, have difficulty focusing, and struggle to complete tasks that require sustained attention. ASCA Attention Deficit Hyperactive assesses behaviors commonly associated with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), including inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity.

BASC Attention Problems assess tendencies to be easily distracted, have difficulty focusing, and struggle to complete tasks that require sustained attention. ASCA Attention Deficit Hyperactive assesses behaviors commonly associated with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), including inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity.

BASC Hyperactivity focuses on excessive motor activity, restlessness, impulsivity, and difficulty remaining still. ASCA Attention Deficit Hyperactive, as noted above, covers both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive elements, reflecting a broader ADHD-related symptom pattern.

BASC Withdrawal measures a child’s tendency to pull back from social interaction, show limited involvement in activities, and appear emotionally distant or introverted. ASCA Avoidant focuses on avoidance driven by fear or anxiety, such as fear of social judgment, criticism, or rejection.

BASC Conduct Problems identifies rule-breaking, oppositional, and potentially aggressive behaviors that violate expected social norms. ASCA Delinquent emphasizes more serious antisocial acts, potentially involving illegal activity or more severe violations of societal rules.

BASC Conduct Problems is a broad measure of disruptive behaviors, which can include aggression, theft, and other norm-violating actions. ASCA Oppositional Defiant zeros in on persistent defiance, hostility, and argumentative behavior directed at authority figures, capturing the classic signs of Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD).

BASC Aggression measures harmful or hostile actions such as fighting, threatening others, or acting violently. ASCA Solitary Aggressive Provocative highlights aggressive behaviors that seem proactively harmful and unprovoked, often initiated independently rather than as a response to provocation.

BASC Aggression focuses on a range of hostile or violent behaviors. ASCA Solitary Aggressive Impulsive captures impulsive, spur-of-the-moment aggressive actions that occur in isolation, reflecting poor impulse control and sudden anger outbursts.

BASC Externalizing encompasses various outwardly directed problem behaviors, including aggression, hyperactivity, and oppositionality. ASCA Overactivity focuses on excessive energy, restlessness, and an inability to settle down, highlighting the high-energy aspects of externalizing behavior but not necessarily all forms of misconduct.

BASC Internalizing measures inwardly focused problems, such as anxiety, depression, somatic complaints, and social withdrawal due to emotional distress. ASCA Underactivity emphasizes low energy, low drive, and a lack of engagement in activities, reflecting a subdued behavior style rather than explicitly anxious or depressed mood states.

Progressive -ing. The annotation covers OCs of the progressive verb form in main lexical verbs occurring in finite verb phrases. Present

Plural -s. The annotation covers OCs of the regular plural number form in nouns, while irregular nominal plurals or plural number forms with other lexical categories (adjectives) were not annotated, as done in previous MOS.

Copula be. The annotation covers OCs of copula be in finite verb phrases, so imperatives and other non-finite forms were not annotated. Copulas in the negative form were tagged because, unlike lexical verbs, the negator does not force the verb be to appear in the base form. This also holds for auxiliary be.
Auxiliary be. The annotation covers OCs of auxiliary be, specifically in progressive and passive contexts.

Article. The annotation covers OCs of (in)definite articles (a(n)/the). Given that the ‘zero article’ was disregarded in previous MOS, it was also disregarded here for comparative purposes. The non-suppliance of an article in an (in)definite OC was tagged as omission. Also, given that both definite and indefinite articles were analysed as a single morpheme in previous MOS, we analysed them similarly, even if we are aware that they are better analysed separately as they do not emerge simultaneously (cf. the discussion in Section 4.4). Selection of one article for the other was tagged as ‘mis-selection’. The forms a/an were understood as spelling variants, so selection of one when the other was expected was not tagged as NTLU. Importantly, determining the OC of the/a(n) is based on information-status distinctions deriving from discourse, i.e., on whether the entity has been previously mentioned in the discourse (i.e., discourse-old, topic) or not (i.e., discourse-new, focus), and therefore whether or not the referent is known to the reader. Articles were annotated independently of the appearance of characters in the picture story, which could give the sense of old information, but technically introduce discoursenew information when retelling the story to a reader. Therefore, ILA considers hearer/reader knowledge (and not speaker knowledge) to determine discourse-old/discourse-new distinctions (cf. Hawkins, 2001).

Irregular past. The annotation covers OCs of the irregular past tense form of lexical verbs only. Similarly to the rationale with irregular plural, cases of misformation (and also oversuppliance) are those where the learner applies the regular past -ed rule to a morphologically past-irregular verb.
Regular past. The annotation covers OCs of the simple past tense -(e)d form of regular lexical verbs.

Possessive. The annotation covers OCs of the genitive structure [noun’s + NP]. Cases showing absence of the apostrophe have been marked as TLU, as we understand that the morpheme has been produced and the apostrophe represents a spelling issue.
